s-10-2.plain_english: The big company has to pick someone named the Data Protection Officer who will help them follow the rules about protecting personal information. This person needs to live in India and report directly to their bosses. They also need a data auditor to check if they are following all the rules properly. The big company must do regular checks on how it handles people's private stuff, just like you might have someone look over your homework to make sure you're doing everything right.

s-11.plain_english: The person whose information we're talking about (we'll call them Customer) can ask their trusted company to show them a summary of their personal data and how it's being used. But there are some exceptions: they don't need to be told about sharing with another trusted company that asks for help investigating a problem.

Companies must change incorrect info, fill out missing details, and update the data when asked by customers. Customers need to tell companies how to contact them so they can erase their personal data. If a company needs to keep some of your data for work reasons or following laws, you won't be deleted.

s-15.plain_english: A customer must follow all laws when using their rights in this act. They can't pretend to be someone else with their personal information. s-28-8.plain_english: The board can't stop you from using your own place or take away things that could make it hard for you to do your work, as long as it doesn't break rules about protecting personal data.
questions: Can the board enter my office if I need to use it for work?
What happens if they want to check something in our equipment room? Can we stop them from taking things?
Is there a risk that they might take important items like computers or documents without permission?
Do I have any say in what the board does with my personal data, even if it's for work purposes?
Can they enter my home to check on something related to our company’s data?
What do we do if they try to take things from our office that aren't part of our equipment but are important to us?
Is there a specific rule about not taking personal items like phones or laptops when checking equipment?
Can I ask the board to leave my workspace if it's causing me problems?

s-28-9.plain_english: The Board can ask police officers or government officials to help them, and they must follow their requests.
questions: In case I need help from a police officer for this board's work, how do I request it?
What happens if the board asks a police officer to check on something related to personal data? Do I have to agree?
How can the Board get assistance from other government officials when dealing with personal data issues?
Do we need permission from the board before asking a police officer for help?
Can any police officer be asked by the Board to assist, or are there specific types of officers who can do it?
If the Board asks someone to check on personal data, what should I expect them to find out?
How does this process work if the Board needs an investigation into a potential leak in our system?
Do we need to give any special instructions when asking for police help with personal data issues?

s-28-10.plain_english: The board can make temporary decisions during their investigation if they think it's needed and write down why. They must let the person involved know about this before making any changes.
questions: Can the board change things without telling anyone?
What happens if someone disagrees with a decision made by the board?
Can the board tell me what I can do to stop them from changing something temporarily?
How long does it take for the board to make decisions during their investigation?
If the board makes an interim order, can they change it later without hearing me again?
What if someone wants to know why the board made a temporary decision? Can they ask?
Can I request that the board not make any changes until I have had time to think about it?
How do I find out what the board has decided during their investigation?

s-28-11.plain_english: After hearing the person involved, if the Board decides that enough information has been gathered and no further investigation is needed, they can decide not to continue the case. Or they can follow the steps outlined in Section 33 instead.
questions: In what situations would the Board choose to stop investigating after hearing the person concerned?
How does Section 33 differ from how the Board handles cases after hearing a party involved?
When might the Board decide not to continue with an investigation and close it, based on reasons recorded in writing?
What are the steps outlined in Section 33 that the Board could choose to follow instead of continuing the inquiry?
Is there any specific reason or criteria the Board must provide for closing an investigation after hearing a party involved?
How does the process differ if the Board decides not to continue with the case versus following section 33?
In what ways can Section 33 help expedite the decision-making process when dealing with cases after hearing parties involved?
Can you give examples of situations where the Board might choose to follow section 33 rather than continuing an investigation?

s-28-12.plain_english: If the Board thinks your complaint isn't real or silly, they can tell you to stop bothering them or make you pay some money as a warning.
questions: What happens if my complaint is considered false by the Board? Can I be charged for filing it?
How much might I have to pay if the Board says my complaint was frivolous?
Do we need to file complaints through an official channel, or can anyone do so without consequences?
Can the Board issue a warning instead of asking us to delete our data in response to a complaint?
If someone files multiple false complaints, what happens then?
What does it mean for a complaint to be considered 'frivolous' by the Board?
How might filing a complaint affect my relationship with the Board going forward?
Can we appeal if the Board decides not to take action on our complaint?

s-29.plain_english: If someone disagrees with something the Board decides about their personal data, they can ask a special group called the Appellate Tribunal to look at it again. They have 60 days to file this appeal and need to pay some money too. If they miss the deadline, they might still be allowed if there's a good reason. The Appellate Tribunal will review what happened and make decisions based on their findings. They must tell everyone involved about any new orders they give. They try to finish all appeals within six months but can explain why if that isn't possible.
questions: Who decides when personal data is used incorrectly?
How long do I have to appeal a Board decision?
What happens if I miss the deadline for appealing?
Can the Appellate Tribunal change what the Board decided?
Where does the Appellate Tribunal send copies of its decisions?
Is there a limit on how long an appeal can take?
Who pays fees when appealing to the Appellate Tribunal?
How quickly should appeals be dealt with by the Appellate Tribunal?

s-29-1.plain_english: If someone is unhappy with a decision made by the Board in your case, you can ask a special group called the Appellate Tribunal to look at it again.
questions: In what situation would I need to appeal against an order from the Board?
How do I file an appeal if I want to challenge something the Board has decided?
What kind of decisions can be appealed by someone under this Act?
Do I have a right to ask for my data back after it was processed by the Board?
Is there a time limit for filing an appeal against the Board's decision?
How many people make up the Appellate Tribunal, and how are they chosen?
What happens if the Appellate Tribunal decides in favor of the Board again?
Do I need to pay any fees to file an appeal?

s-29-2.plain_english: If someone disagrees with an order made about their data, they have to file a formal appeal within 60 days of getting the decision. They need to fill out the appeal in the way it's set up and pay any required fee.
questions: How long do I have to file an appeal after receiving an order?
What form should my appeal be in?
Do I need to pay a fee for filing an appeal, and if so, how much?
Who decides what the forms look like for appeals?
Can I appeal more than once, or is there only one chance to file an appeal?
Is it possible to extend the 60-day deadline for filing an appeal?
What happens if I miss the 60-day deadline for filing an appeal?
Who can decide what constitutes a valid form and manner for filing an appeal?

s-29-3.plain_english: If someone misses the deadline to appeal, they can still do so later as long as they have a good reason and the Appellate Tribunal agrees they should be allowed to appeal after the initial time limit has passed.
questions: Can I appeal if I miss the initial appeal period?
What kind of reasons would make me eligible for an appeal after the deadline?
How does the Appellate Tribunal decide if I have a good reason to appeal later?
Is there any specific information or evidence needed to show they missed the deadline?
Does the Appellate Tribunal require proof that my case is important enough to justify late filing?
What happens if the Appellate Tribunal decides not to allow an appeal after the initial period?
Can I still appeal even if I didn't file a formal request within the initial time frame?
How can I make sure they consider all of my reasons for missing the deadline?

s-29-4.plain_english: If someone appeals a decision from the original tribunal, they can ask for changes in that decision. The higher court will listen to both sides and then decide what to do—keep the original decision, change it slightly, or completely overturn it.
questions: Can I appeal if I don't like how my case was handled?
What happens after I file an appeal? Do they hear me out first?
If I win my appeal, can the original court make changes to their decision?
Does the higher court have to agree with the original court's decision?
How long does it take for them to decide on my appeal?
Can I ask for a specific change in how I was treated during the appeal process?
If they don't hear me out, can I still file an appeal?
What if I disagree with their final decision? Can I do anything else?

s-29-5.plain_english: The special court will give copies of their decisions to both the oversight board and the people who started the appeal, so everyone is informed about what happened.
questions: In case of an appeal, where do I find out about the court's decision?
What information should I expect to receive from the Board after my appeal is heard?
How can I track if the Appellate Tribunal has sent copies of their decisions to all parties involved?
Do I need to check with the Board to confirm they received a copy of the order?
If something goes wrong, who do I contact first about the oversight board's involvement?
Who should I reach out to for more information on how to appeal an order made by the Appellate Tribunal?
How can I ensure that all parties involved receive copies of the court's decision?
Do I need to inform anyone if I want to know what happened in my case after it was heard?

s-29-6.plain_english: If someone files an appeal in front of the Appellate Tribunal, they want their case handled quickly so they can get a final decision within about six months.
questions: How long does the Appellate Tribunal have to make a final decision on my appeal?
Can I expect my appeal to be heard and decided in less than a year?
What happens if the Appellate Tribunal doesn't decide on my case within six months?
Is there anything I can do if I don't get a decision from the Appellate Tribunal after six months?
How does the Appellate Tribunal ensure it handles appeals quickly and efficiently?
Can I appeal again if I'm not satisfied with the first decision made by the Appellate Tribunal?
What should I expect in terms of communication from the Appellate Tribunal during my appeal process?

s-29-7.plain_english: If an appeal can't be resolved by a judge in less than six months, the higher court has to explain why it took so long and what they're doing about it.
questions: Why did my appeal take so long to resolve?
What happened during those six months that delayed our appeal?
Can I expect an update on when my appeal will be decided now that more time has passed?
Who can I contact if I still have questions about the delay in resolving my appeal?
Does this mean my case is permanently stuck or do they plan to resolve it soon?
What actions are being taken by the court to expedite my appeal process?
Can you provide any timeline for when we might expect a decision on our appeal now that more time has passed?
Is there anything I can do to help speed up the resolution of my appeal?

s-29-8.plain_english: The special court can decide any complaints about a decision made by them based on how they usually handle other cases. They follow their own set of rules to hear these appeals.
questions: In which cases does the Appellate Tribunal deal with an appeal?
How do they decide if someone has a right to appeal?
What are some examples of situations where this section might apply?
Do people have to pay anything when appealing to the Appellate Tribunal?
How long can it take for the Appellate Tribunal to make a decision after receiving an appeal?
Can anyone appeal decisions made by the Appellate Tribunal?
If someone disagrees with an appeal, what are their options?
What happens if the Appellate Tribunal decides against the party appealing?

s-29-9.plain_english: If someone appeals a decision made by the Appellate Tribunal in this act, they will follow the rules set out for telecom cases in another law called the Telecom Regulatory Authority of India Act, 1997.
questions: In an appeal case under this act, how do we handle complaints about data privacy issues?
What happens if someone wants to delete their information after an order is made by the Appellate Tribunal?
How can a customer challenge a decision that affects their personal data in court?
If there's a dispute over who owns the right to appeal under this act, what does it mean for telecom cases too?
Can customers get compensation if they lose an appeal related to their privacy rights?
What are the steps involved when someone wants to file an appeal and ensure their data is protected during that process?
How do we resolve conflicts between different laws regarding appeals in personal data matters?
If there's a conflict between this act and another law about how to handle appeals, which one takes precedence?

s-29-10.plain_english: If someone wants to appeal something under this law, they can file their appeal digitally and everything related to it will be handled through a digital system, including receiving the appeal and making decisions about it.
questions: Can I submit my appeal online for faster processing?
Will all communications regarding my appeal be done electronically?
How do I know if my appeal has been received by the Appellate Tribunal?
What happens if there is a hearing for my appeal? Is it conducted virtually or in person?
Can I request to have my case reviewed without having to go through an entire digital process?
If my appeal fails, can I still try to submit another one digitally?
How do I know when the decision on my appeal has been made and how will I be notified of it?
Is there a way to access or download any documents related to my case that are part of the digital process?

s-30.plain_english: If an appellate tribunal makes a decision, they can enforce it like a judge in a regular court would. They have all the same powers to make orders. If the case is about something specific and local, they can send their order to a nearby civil court, which will then handle it as if it were its own decision.
questions: Can an appellate tribunal's decision be enforced like a regular court decree?
What happens if an appellate tribunal needs help enforcing their orders in specific cases?
How can I get my data protected under this act?

Can customers request that their personal information be deleted from company records?
What if a customer wants to appeal an appellate tribunal's decision? How is that done?
Is there a way for customers to get compensation for data breaches?
How does the act ensure that all decisions are made fairly and without bias?

s-31.plain_english: If the Board thinks a problem can be solved by talking it out, they can tell everyone to try resolving their issue through mediation with someone they both choose or that is set up by the rules.
questions: If we have a disagreement and want to solve it without going to court, who decides if we should use mediation?
How do I find a mediator for our dispute?
Do we need special permission from anyone to use mediation?

Why does the law say this must be done by mutual agreement or under existing rules?
Can we choose any mediator we want, or are there specific requirements?
If we decide to mediate, who pays for it?
Do we have to go through mediation before going to court?

s-32.plain_english: The board can accept a promise from anyone that they will follow the rules set by our law book. This promise can be about doing something or not doing something. The board can change this promise if everyone agrees to it. If someone breaks their promise, we can take action against them according to another part of the law.
questions: Can I make a promise to follow your rules and get out of trouble?
If someone makes a promise to do something, can you change that promise later?
What happens if someone breaks their promise to follow our rules?
Can we still take action against someone who broke their promise even though they made a promise to us?
How do I know what promises I have to make and what actions I need to take?
If I break my promise, can you tell me why I did it wrong?
Does the board have to let me explain before taking action against someone who broke their promise?
Can we change our rules if someone makes a promise to follow them?

s-33.plain_english: If someone breaks important rules in our data protection law, they might have to pay money as a punishment. The amount depends on how bad their mistake was, what kind of personal information got mixed up, and if they tried to fix it.
questions: What is the maximum penalty for breaking this act's rules?
How do I know if my breach is significant enough to get a penalty?
Can you explain what 'repetitive nature' means in this context?
If someone realizes they've made a profit from a data breach, does that mean they'll pay more penalties?

How do I know if my response to the penalty is effective and timely?
Is there any chance the penalty won't affect me financially?
Do you think someone who didn't try to fix their mistake will get a lighter penalty?

s-34.plain_english: This section says any money collected as fines for breaking the rules in our act will go into a big pot called the Consolidated Fund of India.
questions: Where does the money from penalties go?
Who collects these fines and where do they put the money?
Is there a specific account or fund where all penalty money goes to?
What is this 'Consolidated Fund of India' used for?
Can we see how much money has been collected in fines so far?

Does collecting fines help pay for public services, like schools or hospitals?
How do people know if they are being fined under this act?

s-35.plain_english: This section says that if someone does something good-hearted under our data protection law, they won't get sued by others. It protects people who work for the government and make decisions based on what's right even if things go wrong.
questions: Can we sue the Central Government for mistakes made in good faith?
Who can be protected from legal action under this section?
Does this mean I won't get sued by others if I do something good for my company based on new data rules?

Can we still sue someone who works for the government if they make a mistake?
Is there any situation where this section doesn't apply, like if I break the law deliberately?
Who decides what is considered 'done in good faith'? Is it just the people doing the work or others too?
Does this mean we can always trust that the government and its workers will make decisions based on our data protection rules?

s-36.plain_english: The government can ask the board and anyone who handles data to give them whatever information they need for our law.
questions: Can the government get all the details about how someone is using my personal info?
If I want, do I have to tell the government everything about what companies are doing with my data?

Can they make sure that all the companies using my info follow our laws properly?
If I give them too much sensitive personal info, will it be safe and not shared with others?
Is there a limit to how long the government can keep asking for this information?
Do I have any say in what kind of data they ask for from these other companies?

s-37.plain_english: The government can tell service providers not to share certain types of information with customers if they've been found guilty of breaking rules multiple times. They can do this after giving the provider a chance to explain and record their decision in writing. The service providers must follow these instructions.
questions: Can the government block access to my data by companies that offer goods or services?
What happens if I'm found guilty of breaking rules multiple times with my company?
How can I get a chance to explain why they shouldn't block my information from being shared?

Does this apply only to computer resources like websites, or does it cover other types of information too?
Who decides what type of information should be blocked from being accessed by others?

s-38.plain_english: This section says that when there are rules from other laws already in place, we add our own rules on top of them. If a new rule conflicts with an old one, we follow our new rules unless it causes problems.
questions: What happens if the Digital Personal Data Protection Act and another law both say different things about personal data? Can you pick which one to use?

How do I know which law is more important between this one and another, like deciding who gets to choose dessert first at a party?
Can someone else's rule override our Digital Personal Data Protection Act rules on personal data if they're older?

s-39.plain_english: This section means that courts can't handle cases about what the Board (a group that makes rules) is allowed to do, and they can't stop the Board from doing its job by giving them an order to not do something.
questions: Can a court decide if the Board did something wrong?

Does this section affect how courts can handle cases involving personal data under the Act?

s-40.plain_english: This law allows the government to create rules that help explain how companies should communicate with customers about their data and ensure they follow certain obligations. It also covers things like who needs to register, what kind of information can be shared for free, how to report a data leak, and how to get your personal info removed if you want it gone.

s-40-1.plain_english: The government can create new rules to help follow the Digital Personal Data Protection Act as long as they don't go against what's in the act itself and after they're published for everyone to see.

s-40-2.plain_english: This provision allows rules to specify how a Data Fiduciary should inform a customer about their rights and obligations, including things like accountability measures for Consent Managers. It also covers what kinds of information must be provided in case of a data breach and when certain duties can be considered fulfilled.

s-41.plain_english: The rules and notifications made by the government under this act must be shared with both houses of parliament within 30 days. If they agree, they can change these rules or say they don't need to be followed at all. The changes will only apply after the agreed-upon modifications are made.
questions: When should I expect to see new government rules and notifications in my inbox?

Can we request that a particular rule or notification be reviewed before making any changes?
Is there a way for me to provide feedback on the government's rules and notifications?

s-42.plain_english: The government can change some rules in a list called 'Schedule' by telling everyone about it, but they can't make penalties stricter than what was originally set.

s-43.plain_english: If there are any problems with how a part of the act works, the government can make new rules to fix them without breaking other parts of the law. These new rules must not go against what's already in the act and they need to be made within three years after the act starts working. The government has to show these new rules to both houses of parliament as soon as possible.

s-44.plain_english: This provision changes some parts of existing laws. It adds a new tribunal under the Digital Personal Data Protection Act that can hear cases related to telecom and airport regulations. It also removes a specific section from the Information Technology Act, and modifies how the Right to Information Act handles personal information.

def-appellate-tribunal.plain_english: This section tells us about a special group called the Appellate Tribunal. It's like a higher court that handles telecom disputes based on rules made by another law.

def-automated.plain_english: This section says that 'automated' refers to anything that can work by itself on a computer based on what it's told, like a program that sorts emails without you having to do it manually.

def-board.plain_english: The 'Board' is a group set up by the government to handle data protection stuff.

def-certain-legitimate-uses.plain_english: This chapter explains that certain legitimate uses refer to what's listed in Section 7. It's about how organizations can use customer data legally.

def-chairperson.plain_english: This section just tells us who the 'Chairperson' is - it's the person in charge of the board. It’s like having a captain for your company’s decision-making team.

def-child.plain_english: This section says a 'child' is anyone under 18 years old. It helps us understand who we need to treat differently when it comes to personal information, like keeping their data safe and asking for permission before using it.

def-consent-manager.plain_english: A Consent Manager is someone you can talk to about your data. They help you decide what information you want shared and how it should be used, and they keep track of all the choices you make.

def-data.plain_english: The term 'data' refers to any kind of information that can be communicated or processed using machines or humans. It includes numbers, text, images, and other forms of data.
questions: In what form is data considered valid for communication?
